entries.content_preview: The Ludwik Kowalski “Learn Cold Fusion” Website Archive Dr. Ludwik Kowalski contributed to the cold fusion field in several ways. He created a website that is both a storehouse of information and a complete report on his work in the field. He conducted experiments and collaborated with other researchers. He understood and commented on the sociology of science issues that arose in the rejection of cold fusion. Dr. Kowalski passed away in October 2021. More information can be found in the memorial obituary “Ludwik Kowalski, Major Contributor to the Cold Fusion,” which appears in Infinite Energy Issue 159. Dr. Kowalski's cold fusion contributions and accomplishments are recorded in his “Learn Cold Fusion” (LCF) website. His motivation in creating the website is described on an introductory webpage as follows: About my "learn cold fusion" project In the fall of 2002, to my surprise, I discovered that the field of cold fusion is still active. This happened at the International Conference on Emerging Nuclear Systems (ICENES2002 in Albuquerque, New Mexico). Several papers presented at this conference were devoted to cold fusion topics. Intrigued by the discovery I started reading about recent cold fusion findings and sharing what I learned with other physics teachers. I have been doing this over the Internet using Montclair State University website: https://msuweb.montclair.edu/~kowalskil/cf/ What follows is a set of items posted, more or less regularly, on that website since October of 2002. The items reflect my own process of learning, mostly from articles published by cold fusion researchers. I am still not convinced that excess heat, discovered by Fleischmann and Pons, is real or that nuclear transmutations can occur at ordinary temperatures. But I do think that time is right for the second evaluation of the entire field. I do not believe that extraordinary findings of hundreds of researchers are products of their imagination or fraud. entries.content_preview: COLD FUSION TECHNOLOGY END ENERGY SCARCITY 1. ONE-PAGE EXECUTIVE VERSION: MODEL 333-A CORE Objective: Establish a reproducible research platform to investigate anomalous heat and nuclear isotopic signatures in Pd–Ni–Zr lattices loaded with deuterium. Core Pillars: Pillar Status Purpose Reproducibility READY Open-source lattice specs allow distributed experimental replication. Purity / Contamination Control MANDATED Ultra-pure D₂ gas, differential vacuum, continuous leak monitoring to minimize background helium/tritium. Energy Consistency / Telemetry ACTIVE Phase-locked phonon excitation aligned with deuterium diffusion; dual-phase calorimetry tracks heat; mass spectrometry monitors ⁴He, ³He, Tritium. Operational Highlights: Dual-phase isoperibolic calorimetry ensures precise heat measurements with a null cell baseline. Temporal correlation aligns phonon pulses with deuterium diffusion to enhance low￾energy tunneling probability. High-resolution mass spectrometry provides isotopic verification for nuclear attribution. Strategic Advantage: Open-source design and distributed replication bypass traditional institutional gatekeeping, providing transparency and accelerating scientific evaluation. 2. PEER-REVIEW STYLE REWRITE Title: Model 333-A Core: A Platform for Correlated Calorimetry and Isotopic Analysis in Pd– Ni–Zr Deuterium Lattices Abstract: We present a conceptual and operational framework for a reproducible experimental system (Model 333-A) designed to investigate correlations between lattice-mediated energy release and nuclear isotope production. The system integrates phase-locked phonon excitation, dual-phase isoperibolic calorimetry, and high-resolution mass spectrometry to provide synchronized telemetry for ⁴He, ³He, and tritium detection. Materials and Methods: Lattice: Pd–Ni–Zr nanostructured powder with high surface area and active site density.
